title: Leader Election, Leases & Fencing
summary: Coordinate single-owner background work safely using consensus leases and monotonic fencing tokens.
body:
Whenever you introduce a single active coordinator—a partition scheduler, shard primary, or compaction driver—two failure modes dominate interviews: split-brain zombie leaders and singleton throughput bottlenecks.

## Why leases alone cannot prevent split-brain
Suppose Worker A acquires a 10-second lease, starts a write, and hits a 15-second stop-the-world GC pause or network stall:
- At `t = 11s`, the lease expires and Worker B legitimately acquires leadership.
- At `t = 15s`, Worker A wakes up, still believing it is leader, and sends its delayed write, corrupting Worker B's newer state.
- Checking wall-clock time on Worker A is unsafe because clocks drift and pauses can occur after the check.

## Monotonic fencing tokens
Pair every leadership lease with a strictly increasing `fencing_token` (epoch number) issued by a consensus store (`etcd`, `ZooKeeper`, Raft, or a transactional DB sequence):
- Worker A receives `token = 34`; when Worker B takes over after expiry, it receives `token = 35`.
- Worker A and Worker B pass their `fencing_token` on every storage mutation or downstream command.
- The target storage records `highest_seen_token = 35` and rejects any write carrying `token < 35`, making zombie writes harmless.

## Prefer partitioned ownership over one global leader
- A single cluster-wide leader caps throughput to one machine and causes a full availability blip during failover.
- Shard coordination across `K` virtual partitions (for example, `64` or `256` timer/job buckets), electing or assigning a lease per partition so failover affects only `1/K` of traffic.
- Tune lease `TTL` (commonly `10-30s`) with renewal at `TTL / 3` to balance fast crash recovery against false failovers during transient network blips.
